strengths: The core walk-stitching idea is clean and well-motivated: composing l independent GRF products with a 2l-level de-convolved modulation function yields an unbiased estimator of the same graph kernel while allowing short, parallel-sampled walks to emulate long ones. Lemma 2.1/3.1 and the connection to (de-)convolutions and Taylor roots of the kernel-generating function (Sec. 3.1) form a coherent and reusable theoretical toolkit.

Generalizing walk termination from Bernoulli halting to arbitrary discrete distributions (Sec. 2.2.2, Algorithm 2) is a natural and useful extension, and the theory covers this general case rather than only the special instantiation.

The paper makes a genuine effort to isolate the effect of stitching itself: the ablation in Fig. 4 (re-using the exact same walk set across degrees) shows accuracy gains that cannot be attributed merely to sampling more independent walks, and the timing breakdown in Fig. 5 distinguishes walk time from stitching time.

Empirical evaluation spans approximation quality (Figs. 2, 7, 8, including large-diameter graphs), speed, and three downstream tasks (graph classification, node clustering, mesh normal interpolation), with per-dataset details and mesh IDs provided in the appendix, supporting reproducibility.

The practical options (sparse Option I, JLT down-projection Option II, matrix-chain multiplication Option III) with explicit complexity analysis (O(N) kernel-vector products for constant l) make the method usable in realistic settings, and the observation about walk-stitching with general termination strategies (Sec. 2.2.3, p_next analysis) directly addresses the known weakness of GRFs on distant node pairs.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis has gaps relative to the claims. The abstract/conclusion promise 'concentration results,' but no concentration bound appears anywhere in the paper. More seriously, the proof of Theorem 3.3 (App. A.3) is sketchy and internally inconsistent: the indexing notation (e.g., 'v_2^t' vs. 2^t) is garbled, and the crucial inequality (18) is justified in a single sentence asserting a 'prefix' characterization of non-zero products that is not carefully proven. Since monotone MSE improvement with stitching degree is a headline theoretical claim, this needs tightening.

The experimental comparison raises fairness concerns. In Figs. 2/3/7/8 the x-axis is 'number of random walks,' but for degree-l GRFs++ it is unclear whether the walk budget is per-factor or total; if per-factor, GRFs++ uses ~l times the sampling compute of the GRF baseline, and some of the reported error improvement may reflect additional computation rather than the stitching mechanism per se. The paper should state and enforce an explicit compute-matched comparison.

Evaluation is narrow: only the graph diffusion kernel is used for the downstream tasks, and the kernel-approximation baselines are limited to regular GRFs. No comparison against other graph-kernel approximation strategies (e.g., Nystrom/landmark methods, randomized eigendecompositions, or the QMC/repelling-walk variants of GRFs by the same line of work) is provided, so it is hard to judge practical significance beyond the GRF family.

Scale is modest: Frobenius-error experiments use graphs of up to ~1272 nodes and the speed study uses only a 500-node random graph. Since a central selling point is efficiency for large graphs on modern accelerators, results on larger, sparser graphs (and an actual GPU timing study) would substantially strengthen the efficiency claims.

Scope and applicability of the de-convolution step are under-discussed: the (2l)-th root / Taylor expansion of g may have limited radius of convergence or non-real coefficients for general coefficient sequences alpha, and no limitations section acknowledges this or other constraints (e.g., the empirical observation that re-using walks violates the independence assumption used in the theory). Code is only promised 'upon acceptance,' limiting reproducibility at review time.

The contribution is incremental relative to the existing GRF literature (Choromanski 2023; Reid et al. 2024a,b): walk-stitching is a composition of the existing mechanism and the generalized termination is a modest generalization, so significance hinges on the experimental evidence, which as noted is not fully compute-matched or broad in baselines.

strengths: The paper targets a genuine, recognized limitation of Graph Random Features (GRFs) — the sequential sampling of long walks and poor modeling of distant node pairs — and the proposed walk-stitching idea (combining independent short walks via an l-fold product of feature matrices) is a clean and natural extension of the GRF framework.

The method preserves unbiasedness, and the connection to 2l-level discrete de-convolutions (Sec. 3.1) gives a simple, general recipe for constructing modulation functions (e.g., f(p) = 1/((2l)^p p!) for the diffusion kernel) that is elegant and easy to implement.

The empirical evaluation covers multiple settings (kernel approximation error, graphs with large diameters, speed, graph classification, node clustering, mesh normal prediction), and the ablation re-using the same walks (Fig. 4) is a thoughtful attempt to isolate the benefit of stitching itself.
The paper is generally readable, the reproducibility statement is detailed, and experimental setups (datasets, hyperparameters, protocols) are documented in the appendix.
weaknesses: The fairness of the central accuracy comparisons is unclear. GRFs++ of degree l consumes l sets of walks per estimator, yet Fig. 2/3/7/8 plot error against 'number of random walks m' without clarifying whether m counts total walks or per-component walks. If GRFs++ uses l times more walks, part of the accuracy gain may simply reflect more computation; only the Poisson-halting comparison controls expected walk length, and the time comparison (Fig. 5) does not clearly establish the claimed efficiency advantage.

The claimed efficiency benefits are not convincingly demonstrated. The assertion that 'as the degree increases, both the walk time and the stitching time decreases' (Sec. 4.1, Fig. 5) is surprising and under-explained — stitching l matrix products should add cost — and the 'no extra computational cost' claims in the abstract/introduction are not rigorously supported.

The theoretical results are weaker than advertised. Theorem 3.3 (monotone MSE improvement) holds only for degrees that are powers of two and only under the standard Bernoulli termination; its proof (App. A.3) is sketchy, with a hard-to-parse expression (Eq. 17) and a key step (Eq. 18) justified in one sentence by 'convolutional properties' and a prefix argument. The conclusion also claims 'concentration results,' but no concentration theorem appears anywhere in the paper.

Empirical support is narrow relative to the generality of the framework: nearly all experiments use only the diffusion kernel, graphs are small (mostly N <= 1272), and the only baseline is regular GRFs. There are no comparisons against other scalable kernel-approximation approaches (e.g., Nyström, sketching, or exact computation feasibility on these graph sizes), so the practical significance beyond the GRF line is hard to gauge.

The practice of re-using the same set of walks violates the independence required for unbiasedness, yet it is used in downstream experiments (GRF++r, Tab. 5). While honestly acknowledged, this creates a disconnect between the theory and what is actually evaluated, and no analysis is given of the bias introduced.

The narrative that stitching 'emulates' long walks is loose: independent short walks joined at proxy vertices constitute a different stochastic process than a single Markov walk, and the paper does not quantify when the stitched estimator inherits (rather than merely bounds) the quality of long-walk estimators.

Reproducibility is weakened by the absence of released code ('we will open source the code upon acceptance'), and there are presentation defects: notation inconsistencies in the appendix (e.g., v_{2^t} vs v_{2l} indices in Eq. 16-17), typos ('walk-stitchng', 'predicion'), and imprecise statements (Lemma 2.1's condition vs. its 'more general version').

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine limitation of regular GRFs (Choromanski 2023; Reid et al. 2024b): the reliance on long, inherently sequential random walks, which are poorly suited to modern accelerators and yield poor estimates for distant node pairs. The proposed walk-stitching mechanism is a clean and natural solution, and the connection to 2l-level discrete de-convolutions of the kernel coefficient sequence (Lemma 2.1/3.1, Sec. 3.1) is elegant and gives a practical algorithm (take the (2l)-th root of the kernel's generating function) for computing modulation functions.

The generalization of the Bernoulli walk-termination scheme to arbitrary distributions on walk lengths (Sec. 2.2.2, Algorithm 2) is a nice, well-motivated contribution, and the Poisson termination strategy is shown empirically to improve accuracy at no extra computational cost.

The paper covers both theory and practice: unbiasedness of the (l, P)-GRFs++ estimator is proven for general termination distributions, a compact MSE characterization is given for l = 2 (Lemma 3.2), and a monotonicity result in the stitching degree is stated (Theorem 3.3).

Empirical evaluation is reasonably broad: kernel approximation error on eight synthetic/real graphs, a targeted study on large-diameter graphs (diameters up to 159), a timing breakdown (walk time vs. stitching time), and three downstream tasks (graph classification on TUDataset benchmarks, spectral node clustering, and mesh normal-field prediction on 40 Thingi10K meshes). The ablation in Fig. 4 (re-using the exact same walk set) cleanly isolates the benefit of stitching itself.
The reproducibility statement is detailed, datasets and graph construction procedures are specified, and the algorithmic modifications over Algorithm 1 are described precisely enough to reimplement.
weaknesses: Several theoretical proofs are questionable or incomplete. In the proof of Lemma 3.2 (App. A.2), step 5 claims 'symmetry of X1 and X2' justified by entries being dot-products of feature vectors — but X1 and X2 are built from independently sampled walk sets and are generally not equal, nor is it clear the claimed symmetry/transposition relation E[X2_2] = E[X2_1]^T holds as written; the chain of equalities appears to contain a gap. The proof of Theorem 3.3 (App. A.3) is very sketchy: the key inequality (18) is asserted to follow from 'convolutional properties' and a prefix argument without a rigorous non-negative-correlation argument, and the notation is inconsistent (v_{2^l} vs. v_{2^t}). Additionally, the conclusion claims 'concentration results', but no actual concentration bound appears anywhere in the paper — only MSE identities. The monotonicity result also holds only for degrees that are powers of two and only under the standard Bernoulli termination, limiting its reach.

The experimental scale is modest: timing experiments use random graphs of only 500 nodes, kernel-approximation graphs have N ≤ 1272, and all downstream experiments use relatively small graphs/meshes. Given that the central selling point is computational efficiency on large graphs, no evidence on graphs with N in the tens of thousands or beyond is provided, so scalability claims remain untested.

Empirical claims are mostly restricted to the diffusion kernel, even though the theory (Sec. 3.1) nominally applies to any kernel whose generating function admits a computable (2l)-th root Taylor expansion. No experiments cover other kernel classes (e.g., p-step random walk, regularized Laplacian), so the generality of the method is not demonstrated.

Variance behavior is under-analyzed: while stitching improves bias-like reachability, the load scaling involves products of f(p)-terms that can inflate variance for some kernels/graphs; there is no analysis or experiment indicating when higher l could hurt, beyond the (partially proven) powers-of-two monotonicity claim.

The variance-reducing heuristic of re-using the same walk set (which breaks the independence required for unbiasedness) is used in downstream results (GRF++r in Tables 2 and 5) without any theoretical justification, and its empirical advantage over independent walks is small (e.g., GRF++ consistently outperforms GRF++r in Table 5), weakening the practical relevance of that ablation.

Presentation issues reduce polish: the conclusion of the paper is duplicated almost verbatim in the introduction (pages 1-2), there are typos ('predicion', 'walk-stitchng', inconsistent 'GRF++'/'GRFs++' naming), the graph classification figure (Fig. 6) shows only aggregate bars without error bars or statistical tests, and code is promised only 'upon acceptance' rather than provided.

The novelty is incremental relative to the existing GRF line of work (Choromanski 2023; Reid et al. 2024a,b; Choromanski et al. 2025): walk-stitching and general termination are natural extensions of that framework, and the paper is positioned almost entirely against regular GRFs rather than against a broader set of scalable graph-kernel approximation baselines.

strengths: The walk-stitching idea is well-motivated: regular GRFs require long, sequential random walks, which is both an accelerator-unfriendly procedure and a statistical bottleneck for distant node pairs. Stitching shorter walks via a 2l-level de-convolution of the modulation function is an elegant framing that connects kernel construction to power series roots, and yields simple closed forms for diffusion kernels (f(p) = λ^p/((2l)^p p!)).

The theoretical treatment is substantive: Lemma 3.1 generalizes unbiasedness to both stitching and arbitrary termination distributions (Algorithm 2 subsuming the Bernoulli scheme), Lemma 3.2 gives a compact MSE formula for l=2, and Theorem 3.3 proves monotone MSE improvement with stitching degree (for powers of two). The connection between termination distributions and importance re-weighting by τ(k)=P(X≥k) is clean.

Experiments are broad: kernel approximation error across eight graphs, a dedicated long-distance evaluation on large-diameter graphs (diameters up to 159), ablations separating the stitching benefit from walk re-use, runtime comparisons against brute-force kernel construction, and four downstream tasks (ViT attention masking, GraphGPS positional encodings, node clustering, mesh normal prediction), plus approximation of non-diffusion kernels ((I−W)^{-1}, (I−W²)^{-1}, exp(W²)).

A reproducibility statement is provided with explicit dataset construction procedures, hyperparameter settings, and an open-source implementation; baseline setups follow Reid et al. (2024b) exactly, aiding comparability.
weaknesses: The proof of Theorem 3.3 (the headline 'stitching more improves approximation' result) is not fully rigorous. The key step (Eq. 18) is justified by a one-line assertion that 'the product of two X-variables ... is not identically zero if and only if one of the walks is a prefix of another one,' without a careful argument; the displayed estimators in Eqs. 16-17 contain notation errors (e.g., v_{2^l} vs v_{2^t}, apparent corruption in Eq. 17), and the theorem is restricted to powers-of-two degrees and standard (Bernoulli) termination only.

Fairness of the efficiency claims deserves scrutiny. GRFs++ of degree l requires l independent (K₁,K₂) instantiations, i.e., roughly l times the walk budget and l matrix factors; Theorem 3.3 shows MSE improves with l at fixed m and p_halt, but no result (or clean analysis) characterizes error as a function of total computational cost. The runtime experiments (scaled p_halt × l) partially address this but are limited to 500-node random graphs and mesh tasks; the efficiency claim 'trading sequential sampling for parallel computation' is plausible but not rigorously quantified.

Practical applicability of the de-convolution construction beyond diffusion kernels is underspecified. For the general (l, P)-GRFs++ mechanism, the (2l)-th root's Taylor coefficients must exist and be computable; how f was computed for the (I−W)^{-1} and (I−W²)^{-1} experiments, and whether numerical de-convolution is stable, is not discussed.

The empirical practice of re-using the same walk set across stitching components (GRF++r) breaks the unbiasedness that the theory emphasizes, yet it is used in several downstream experiments; this tension is acknowledged only informally ('empirically we find it performs well') and could mislead readers about which variant guarantees unbiasedness.

Presentation issues: inconsistent notation and figures (K(W)=exp(W²/4) in Sec. 4 vs exp(W²) in B.6 and Fig. 11; (I−W)^{-4} vs (I−W)^{-1} mismatch between text and Fig. 9 caption; 'GRFs++' vs 'GRF++' used interchangeably; Eq. 5-6 formatting), typos ('our model two large scale datasets', 'which is' constructions), and Eq. 2's convergence condition ('∥W∥∞ small enough') is imprecise. Several such errors appear in the statements of theoretical results, reducing confidence.

The core contribution is an incremental refinement of the GRF line (Choromanski 2023; Reid et al. 2024a,b) rather than a new mechanism; the impact is limited by the restriction to intra-graph node kernels in most experiments, and graph classification comparisons are conceded to be 'not directly comparable' with inter-graph kernel baselines.

strengths: The core idea of walk-stitching — composing several short, independently sampled walks to emulate longer walks while provably preserving unbiasedness — is a sensible and practically motivated improvement over regular GRFs, directly targeting the well-known weakness that distant node pairs are poorly modeled when walks do not intersect.

The unification of walk termination into general discrete distributions P (with Algorithm 1 as a special case of Algorithm 2) is a clean generalization, and the connection to 2l-level (de-)convolutions of the modulation function and Taylor roots of the kernel's generating function is a nice conceptual framing (Sec. 2.2.1, Sec. 3.1).

The evaluation is broad: kernel approximation error on many graphs, distant-pair estimation on large-diameter graphs, and several downstream tasks (mesh normal prediction, node clustering, graph classification, ViT masking, GraphGPS positional encodings), with runtime comparisons against brute-force and Al-Mohy baselines.

Hyperparameters in head-to-head comparisons (e.g., scaled halting probability p_halt × l for a fixed average walk length) are chosen with an apparent eye toward fairness, and the ablation re-using identical walks isolates the stitching benefit.
Reproducibility statement enumerates datasets, graph-construction procedures, and proof locations; the underlying GRF codebase from prior work is referenced.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is thin and not fully rigorous. Lemma 3.1's proof (App. A.1) is essentially 'similar analysis' to Reid et al. (2024b), and the displayed derivation is internally inconsistent: Eq. (10) contains survival-probability and 1/τ factors that vanish without justification in the transition to Eqs. (11)-(12). Theorem 3.3's proof is sketchier still — it relies on an informal claim about products of X-variables being nonzero 'if and only if one walk is a prefix of another' (App. A.3, Eq. 18), which is asserted rather than proven and is central to the monotonicity claim. Notably, the theorem only covers powers-of-two degrees with standard termination, so the theory does not cover most of the configurations used in the experiments (e.g., degrees 3, 5, 6; Poisson termination).

Claims of variance/accuracy improvement are asserted more than demonstrated. The abstract claims general termination schemes improve accuracy 'without incurring extra computational cost' and Sec. 2.2.1 claims a probability lower bound 'independent of p_next', but neither claim is formalized. Lemma 3.2 gives an MSE formula only for l = 2, and even the claimed monotonicity (Theorem 3.3) is unproven in general. No concentration bounds appear despite the conclusion asserting 'we provide concentration results'.

Downstream gains are marginal and not clearly attributable. The ViT experiment improves ImageNet accuracy from 80.10 to 80.31 and Places365 from 55.78 to 56.03 — within typical seed noise, and no confidence intervals or seed counts are reported for these tables. GraphGPS improvements are similarly small (e.g., 26.88 → 26.61 on Peptides-func) and no comparison against standard LapPE/RWSE baselines is given, making the 'extends well beyond kernel approximation' claim weakly supported.

Experimental comparisons are predominantly against regular GRFs rather than strong external baselines. The graph classification comparison to 20 kernels/GNNs is acknowledged by the authors to be 'not directly comparable' (intra-graph vs inter-graph kernels), yet it is used to position GRF++ as competitive. Kernel-approximation quality is never benchmarked against alternative sparse approximations (e.g., truncated Taylor expansions, Nyström), so the practical advantage over simple alternatives is unquantified.

Several experimental details undermine confidence: Fig. 7/8 y-axis ranges are implausible for 'relative Frobenius norm error' (values of 10^1–10^3 with asymptotes that don't approach zero), suggesting plots show unnormalized errors or mislabeled axes. Table 1 speedups vs brute force are expected for any approximation method and do not establish an advantage of GRFs++ over GRFs. The claim that stitching time 'decreases' with degree (Sec. 4.1) contradicts the cost model of multiplying l sparse matrices.

The method's costs are understated. Option I requires products of sparse matrices, which are not guaranteed to remain sparse; the O(N) multiplication claim (Option III) silently assumes constant l and constant density. The de-convolution step requires computing the (2l)-th root of the kernel's generating function and its Taylor coefficients, which need not exist, be real-valued, or be efficiently computable in general — only the diffusion kernel admits a simple closed form, and indeed nearly all experiments use the diffusion kernel.

Writing and notation are careless: Algorithm 1 uses ρ/ξ while the surrounding text uses f/φ without reconciling them; Eq. (16)-(17) use v^{2l} vs v_{2^t} inconsistently; Eq. (3)'s index appears garbled ('Y2'/'Y2+1' for even/odd l); 'GRF++' vs 'GRFs++' alternate throughout; 'Al Mohy' is a mangled citation of Al-Mohy & Higham. The reproducibility statement ends mid-sentence ('we open source our implementation at') with no repository URL provided, so code availability is unverifiable.

Originality is limited: both ingredients (composition of walk-based estimators and arbitrary walk-length distributions preserving unbiasedness) are direct, predictable extensions of the GRF framework of Choromanski (2023) and Reid et al. (2024b), and the paper positions itself as such. The contribution is an incremental refinement rather than a new understanding or a new problem capability.

strengths: The paper addresses genuine, well-motivated limitations of Graph Random Features (GRFs): the difficulty of modeling distant node pairs and the sequential, accelerator-unfriendly sampling of long random walks. Walk-stitching, which composes independent short walks while preserving unbiasedness via 2l-level (de-)convolutions of the modulation function, is a clean and sensible remedy, and the connection to taking (2l)-th roots of the kernel's generating function (Sec. 3.1) is elegant.

The theoretical treatment of the core mechanism is reasonable: Lemma 3.1 (unbiasedness under general termination distributions) and Lemma 3.2 (compact MSE form for l=2) are clearly stated with proofs in the appendix, and Algorithm 2 nicely generalizes the Bernoulli halting scheme to arbitrary efficiently-samplable length distributions.

The empirical evaluation is broad: kernel approximation error on synthetic and real graphs (Figs. 2, 7, 8, 9-11), long-range estimation on large-diameter graphs, runtime/scalability vs. brute force (Tab. 1, Fig. 6), and four downstream tasks (graph classification, node clustering, mesh normal prediction, ViT attention masking, GraphGPS positional encodings). Consistent, if modest, improvements over regular GRFs are reported across settings.

The computational story is credible: trading sequential long-walk sampling for parallel short-walk sampling plus matrix products, with sparsity/associativity arguments (Options I-III) and measured speedups (1.7x-3x over brute force).
The reproducibility discussion lists datasets, graph construction procedures, and hyperparameters in reasonable detail (App. B, D).
weaknesses: Overclaiming relative to delivered theory: the abstract and conclusion advertise 'concentration results', but no concentration inequality is actually proven anywhere in the paper; the theory consists of unbiasedness, an MSE expression, and a monotonicity claim. The claimed theoretical contribution should be scaled back or the missing concentration analysis provided.

The proof of Theorem 3.3 (MSE monotonicity in stitching degree) is incomplete. The key step, Eq. (18), is asserted to 'follow from the convolutional properties of the modulation function and the fact that the product of two X-variables... is not identically zero iff one of the walks is a prefix of another one', which does not constitute a proof of the stated expectation inequality. The proof also contains notation inconsistencies (e.g., v_2^l vs v_{2^t}), suggesting it was not carefully checked.

Walk reuse breaks the unbiasedness guarantee: the theory requires independent walk sets across the l components, yet the 're-using the same set of random walks' variant (GRF++r) is used in headline downstream tables (Tabs. 2, 10) and is even reported to outperform the unbiased variant in some cases. The paper should more clearly separate biased heuristics from the theoretically-grounded method.

Error is reported against the number of walks m, but degree-l GRFs++ performs l matrix products per estimate; error-vs-compute (FLOPs/wall-clock) comparisons against regular GRFs would be the fairer basis for the efficiency claims. The speed analysis (Fig. 5b) partially addresses this but is on a single random-graph setting.

Downstream gains are small and significance is rarely established: e.g., ViT improvements of +0.21/+0.25 points and GraphGPS gains of 0.1-1.7 points are reported without confidence intervals or seeds; the graph classification comparison mixes intra-graph node kernels with inter-graph graph kernels, which the authors themselves concede is 'not directly comparable', yet the methods are still ranked in Tabs. 8-9.

Reproducibility statement is incomplete: the sentence 'Finally, we open source our implementation at' is left unfinished with no URL. For a methods paper whose utility rests on implementation, this is a material gap.

Citation hygiene issues undermine confidence: several references appear dubious or incorrectly dated (e.g., 'Kim et al., 2026', 'Yannick-S ... Commit snapshot as of June 26, 2026', a 2026 Expert Systems with Applications DOI cited as 2025), and there is no explicit limitations section discussing when stitching may fail (e.g., very low-degree/fragmented graphs, cost of de-convolution when the (2l)-th root has no closed form).

The framing as resolving 'long-standing limitations' somewhat overstates novelty: the construction is a fairly natural composition trick within the existing GRF framework (Choromanski 2023; Reid et al. 2024b), and the paper would benefit from more explicitly delineating which components are new versus inherited.
